title: The Brothers Karamazov
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
openingChapterLabel: Book I, Chapter 1 — Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov
openingText: Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov was the third son of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov. In his day Fyodor Pavlovitch was a landowner well known in our district, and people here still remember him for his gloomy, tragic death, which happened thirteen years ago. I will describe it in its proper place. For now I will say only this. This “landowner”—that is what we called him, though he hardly spent a day of his life on his own estate—was a strange type, yet quite a common one: a man both abject and vicious and, at the same time, senseless. Still, he was one of those senseless men who handle their worldly affairs very well and, it seems, nothing else. Take Fyodor Pavlovitch. He started with next to nothing. His estate was tiny. He ran from one man’s dinner table to another and clung to his hosts as a toady. Yet when he died, it turned out he had a hundred thousand roubles in cash. And all the while he was one of the most senseless, fantastical fellows in the whole district. I repeat, this was not stupidity. Most of these fantastical fellows are shrewd and intelligent enough. It was just senselessness, and a peculiarly national form of it.
about:
The Brothers Karamazov follows a divided family in a Russian provincial town. Fyodor Pavlovich, a neglectful and provocative father, disputes money with his eldest son Dmitri; both pursue Grushenka. Ivan questions religious belief and moral responsibility. Alyosha, a monastery novice, moves between his spiritual teacher Zosima and a family in growing distress. Their conflicts become a murder investigation and a trial.

Published in 1880, the novel comprises four parts, twelve books and an epilogue. Its author’s preface describes it as the first of two planned novels about Alyosha. The narrative moves between intimate conversations, comic scandal, religious teaching and legal argument. The narrator belongs to the town and sometimes reports rumours rather than established facts.

The long debates matter because their speakers must also act. Follow what each person believes, what each wants others to believe, and what happens when those convictions meet another person’s suffering. Russian characters may be called by a first name, a patronymic or an affectionate name: Alexey is Alyosha, Dmitri is Mitya, Katerina is Katya and Agrafena is Grushenka.

angleCards.title: Faith and doubt
angleCards.text: Ivan challenges attempts to justify the suffering of children. Alyosha listens as a believer who is also disturbed by what he hears. Watch how their affection and disagreement coexist.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Ivan’s challenge to faith and Alyosha’s response without assuming either can be reduced to a single doctrine.

angleCards.title: The Grand Inquisitor
angleCards.text: Ivan’s imagined story places Christ in sixteenth-century Seville. The Inquisitor argues that people would trade freedom for bread, certainty and authority. Read it as a story told by one brother to another, as well as a philosophical challenge.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand how the Grand Inquisitor connects freedom, religious authority and the relationship between the brothers.

angleCards.title: Desire and responsibility
angleCards.text: The brothers are often associated with passion, reason and faith, but each is more complicated than that summary. Follow the distance between a wish, a threat, an action and responsibility for another person.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare the brothers’ choices and ask how the novel distinguishes legal guilt from moral responsibility.

angleCards.title: Love in practice
angleCards.text: Zosima distinguishes active love from the comforting idea of loving humanity. His teaching invites comparison with Ivan’s objections, but the reader must judge what it can answer.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to test Zosima’s teaching against the encounters and choices elsewhere in the novel.

cast.name: Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov
cast.description: A wealthy landowner who neglected his three sons. He is provocative, calculating and sometimes unexpectedly vulnerable. His quarrel with Dmitri concerns both money and Grushenka. The accounts of Dmitri’s inheritance are disputed; distinguish his father’s claims from the narrator’s and Dmitri’s.

cast.name: Dmitri Karamazov
cast.description: A former officer of twenty-eight, also called Mitya. He is engaged to Katerina Ivanovna and passionately drawn to Grushenka. His extravagant spending, violent anger and longing to act honourably repeatedly collide.

cast.name: Ivan Karamazov
cast.description: A twenty-three-year-old intellectual who questions the relation between faith, freedom and morality. His arguments draw the attention of both Alyosha and Smerdyakov. His feelings are not always as controlled as his conversation.

cast.name: Alexey Karamazov
cast.description: Usually called Alyosha. He is twenty and lives at the monastery under Zosima’s guidance. He listens sympathetically but can also judge, fear and misunderstand. The author’s preface identifies him as the intended hero.

cast.name: Father Zosima
cast.description: A starets: a monk sought out for spiritual guidance. He teaches responsibility for others and love expressed through action. His advice sends Alyosha into the world beyond the monastery.

cast.name: Pavel Smerdyakov
cast.description: The cook in Fyodor Pavlovich’s household, raised by Grigory and Marfa after his mother Lizaveta’s death. He has epilepsy and is widely suspected to be Fyodor Pavlovich’s son. He listens closely to Ivan and develops arguments of his own.

whyItMatters.title: An argument lived through
whyItMatters.body: The debates about God and suffering do not take place outside the plot. Their speakers are brothers, lovers, servants and teachers with conflicting needs. Consider what an argument reveals about its speaker, and what later choices do to its apparent certainty.

whyItMatters.title: What does a family owe?
whyItMatters.body: The father’s neglect makes the question of filial duty difficult. The novel asks what people owe a parent who has failed them, and whether resentment changes that obligation. Financial claims, humiliation, dependence and affection are entangled.

whyItMatters.title: Evidence and interpretation
whyItMatters.body: A murder mystery becomes an inquiry into how people construct explanations. Witnesses, gossip and courtroom speeches do not all carry the same authority. The narrator’s qualifications and uncertainties matter, as do the events that resist a convincing story.
